content.body:
The Mk IXc model Spitfire was the RAF's answer to Germany's early Fw 190 "A" series "Butcherbird" fighter. Climb rate, top speed, and ammo load out were all improved markedly over the Mk Vb, producing a faster, much quicker climbing Spitfire with twice the 20 mm cannon rounds to expend in combat compared to its immediate predecessor in the Mk Vb. The even later E wing variant replaced the two .303 light machineguns with a .50 caliber heavy machine gun in each wing, increasing its hitting power over even shorter required firing solutions.
When later variants were deployed into theaters of conflict, the IX model still enjoyed more combat success than any other Spitfire because its combination of climb, speed, and turn rate had produced almost an ideal configuration, and it was available in large numbers as well. Models that followed the IX were notably faster but suffered in the turning role as a result of increased weight and wing loading, extending out beyond what might arguably be called ideal when one considers the still dominant nature of dogfighting in the realms of air to air combat during the typical WWII fighter combat experience.
As the war moved East into Germany, the Spitfire's weakness was finally exposed: it lacked the fuel capacity to penetrate deeply enough into German airspace to fight and return home to Allied bases, which were still a long way from the eastern reaches of the German homeland.
